scenes.label: PHAISTOS, CRETE, 1908
lines: In 1908, a clay disc turned up in the ruins of a palace on Crete.
Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier found it on July 3rd, at Phaistos.

scenes.label: THE DISC
lines: It's about sixteen centimetres across, with writing spiralling over both sides.
Over 240 signs, made from 45 different symbols.

scenes.label: STAMPED, NOT SCRATCHED
lines: And they weren't scratched in. Each sign was pressed into the soft clay with a stamp.
That's printing, thousands of years before Gutenberg.

scenes.label: UNREADABLE
lines: There is no other text like it, so nobody has ever been able to read it.
Its age has never been tested scientifically. In 2008, one expert even suggested it could be a fake.

scenes.label: HERAKLION MUSEUM
lines: Most archaeologists believe it's real. Today it sits in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.
Follow for one mystery every day.

youtube.title: This 3,600-year-old disc was printed with stamps. Nobody can read it. #shorts
youtube.description:
On 3 July 1908 the Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier found a fired-clay disc, about 16 cm across, at the Minoan palace of Phaistos on Crete. Its two sides carry a spiral of over 240 sign tokens (sources give 241 or 242) made from 45 distinct signs, each pressed into the soft clay with a stamp before firing, an early form of movable-type printing. Its date is disputed, with most estimates in the Minoan Bronze Age. With no comparable text, it remains undeciphered. In 2008 Jerome Eisenberg suggested it might be a forgery, noting it has never been dated by thermoluminescence; most archaeologists accept it as authentic. It is kept in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum. Opening photo from Wikimedia Commons (credit below); all other visuals are original illustrations, except photo scenes credited on screen.
